metadata.title: Assessment Framework PIRLS 2016 2nd Edition
metadata.venue: TIMSS & PIRLS International Study Center (Boston College) / IEA

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This document is an assessment framework describing how PIRLS 2016, PIRLS Literacy, and ePIRLS are designed and how reading achievement is scaled and reported; it does not provide an analytic dataset or an empirical model that would require analyst-applied student or replicate weights. PIRLS uses a matrix sampling design (booklets assigned via systematic rotation/randomized procedures) and then applies item response theory scaling to place responses on the PIRLS achievement scale, including linking across cycles (2001, 2006, 2011, 2016). Because the framework does not specify weight variables (e.g., student sampling weights) or replicate-weight methods, weight usage cannot be confirmed from the text. For users of PIRLS microdata, the appropriate complex survey design weights and replicate weights are typically required for variance estimation, but this framework edition focuses on instrument and scaling procedures rather than reporting the weight variable names.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This is a framework/assessment-design document rather than an empirical analysis paper predicting an outcome from student-level data. It describes how reading achievement is scaled using item response theory and how booklets/tasks are sampled, but it does not report a plausible-values (PV) generation or PV-based analytic strategy for a dependent variable. Missing-data handling is therefore not specified because no estimation model with missingness assumptions is evaluated in this text.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used for assessment design: PIRLS targets students in their fourth year of schooling (ISCED Level 1-based target grade), with a recommendation to assess the next higher grade if the average age of fourth grade students at testing is less than 9.5 years. The framework specifies matrix sampling/booklet assignment procedures (systematic booklet assembly and rotation; ePIRLS task combinations distributed so that ~1/12 of students per country respond to each combination), but it does not provide an analytic sample size or country-level inclusion/exclusion criteria.

data.outcome_summary: This PIRLS 2016 Assessment Framework (2nd edition) specifies the construct definition and measurement design for PIRLS, PIRLS Literacy, and ePIRLS rather than reporting empirical predictive results. PIRLS assesses fourth-year students’ reading literacy on a common achievement scale, integrating two reading purposes (literary experience; acquire and use information) and four comprehension processes (retrieve explicitly stated information; make straightforward inferences; interpret and integrate; evaluate and critique). PIRLS and PIRLS Literacy use a matrix sampling design: each student receives two 40-minute blocks from a set of passage/item blocks, enabling broad coverage with limited testing time per student. Achievement is placed on the PIRLS scale using item response theory scaling and linking across cycles (2001, 2006, 2011, 2016). ePIRLS extends PIRLS to online informational reading using computer-based tasks in a simulated Internet environment, with task combinations randomly distributed and scaled via item response theory.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This extraction is for an official IEA/OECD-style assessment framework document, not an empirical study with an analytic sample, model training, or reported performance metrics. As a result, fields such as total_students, country-level sample sizes, PV handling, missing-data handling, and ML techniques are not applicable or not reported in the text. The document’s value is methodological: it defines what is measured (reading literacy construct), how it is measured (booklet/task design, question types, scoring procedures), and how results are scaled and linked across assessment cycles.
